tldr: This paper presents LAC, a whole-body reinforcement learning controller that independently modulates translational and rotational stiffness (compliance) in response to external forces and couples applied to a humanoid's upper body. On real hardware, it achieves compliant physical interactions involving whole-body stepping and posture adjustment.
overview:
For humanoid robots to collaborate with humans or handle fragile objects, compliance—the ability to yield naturally to external forces—is essential. However, most existing controllers either stubbornly reject external forces as disturbances or restrict compliance to translational motion on a few specific links, such as the hands. In particular, independently controlling linear and angular stiffness remained an unsolved challenge. For instance, when someone twists the robot's wrist, it should yield in rotation while maintaining its position; conversely, when carrying an object on its arm, it should remain stiff in orientation to keep the surface level.

To address this, the authors developed LAC, a whole-body controller that accepts linear and angular stiffness commands. The key lies in how the training data is synthesized. From forces and couples (torques) applied to links, the method computes physically consistent virtual torques through the passive deflection of the arm's kinematic chain. It then combines virtual admittance control with whole-body inverse kinematics (IK) to synthesize a large volume of whole-body target motions offline. Using this augmented dataset, a single policy is trained via teacher-student reinforcement learning, relying solely on proprioceptive sensory information such as joint positions and velocities.

Evaluations in simulation and on a 23-DoF humanoid robot (Unitree G1) confirmed that the policy compliantly yields across the whole body to forces and couples on various upper-body locations, monotonically modulating its response according to commanded stiffness. Furthermore, its effectiveness was demonstrated in whole-body collaborative tasks (loco-manipulation) via VR teleoperation, including object carrying and door opening.
contributions: A learning-based whole-body controller that compliantly responds to external forces and couples applied to various upper-body links using whole-body degrees of freedom, including the legs.
The first demonstration, in both simulation and on real hardware, of independently and continuously modulating both linear and angular stiffness via explicit commands in a humanoid robot.

A data synthesis method for angular compliance that references the passive deflection of the entire downstream kinematic chain rather than isolated links, ensuring physical feasibility and observability from proprioceptive sensors.

sections.heading: Why Humanoids Need Both Yielding Compliance and Posture Maintenance
sections.summary: To collaborate with humans and handle delicate objects in the real world, robots need compliance control that yields to external forces rather than simply rejecting them. This paper introduces LAC, a controller that takes independent commands for linear and angular stiffness to yield across the upper body while balancing with the entire body.
sections.details:
Humanoid control is transitioning from simply mimicking human motions to performing real-world tasks. However, most conventional motion-tracking controllers treat external forces as disturbances to be rejected, stiffly resisting them. While this behavior is fine for tasks requiring force resistance, it generates dangerously excessive forces when cooperating hand-in-hand with people or carrying fragile items.

At the same time, granting compliance only in position (translation) is insufficient. For example, during grasp-like physical contacts where a human twists the robot's hand or turns a doorknob, the robot should hold its hand position while yielding smoothly to the twisting torque (low angular stiffness, high linear stiffness). Conversely, when supporting an object on its forearm, it needs to maintain a horizontal orientation so the object does not slide off (high angular stiffness). Linear and angular stiffness must therefore be commanded independently.

Achieving this through reinforcement learning presents a major challenge: how to generate physically plausible target training data that can be observed from the robot's proprioceptive sensors (such as joint encoders). In translation, displacing links like rigid bodies works well. However, rotational compliance manifests as deflections across the arm's entire joint chain. If target rotations were set proportionally to torques around a link's center of mass, applying the same force on opposite sides of the center of mass would flip the torque direction, directly contradicting the actual joint deflection direction and making learning physically impossible.

LAC (Linear and Angular Compliance) overcomes this problem, achieving the first learning-based whole-body controller capable of independently modulating linear and angular stiffness across the upper body.

sections.heading: From Classical Impedance to RL: Why Angular Compliance Was Difficult
sections.summary: Research has advanced from classical impedance control to recent reinforcement learning approaches for quadrupedal and bipedal compliance. However, existing humanoid methods have been limited to a few links and translational compliance, leaving commanded angular compliance an unaddressed domain.
sections.details:
Compliant control has a rich history, including hybrid position/force control for direct force regulation and impedance control for realizing virtual spring-damper dynamics. Recently, reinforcement learning approaches have expanded to legged robots, exploring techniques such as relaxing tracking rewards under external forces or tracking virtual impedance behaviors.

Compliant control has also been explored on humanoid robots, but with critical limitations:
- SoftMimic: Synthesizes motions offline according to external forces and stiffness using whole-body IK, then trains via imitation learning. However, it applies forces to only a single end-effector link per clip, and commanded angular compliance was never experimentally verified.
- GentleHumanoid: Introduces a spring model on arm links to keep contact forces within a safe range, but handles only translation; the lower body attempts to preserve the original motion rather than contributing to compliant responses.
- CHIP: Generates hindsight goals by applying forces to end-effectors, but is also restricted to translational responses at the hands.

In this way, prior methods restricted compliant responses to a small set of links and failed to achieve commanded angular compliance with coordinated whole-body participation involving the lower body.

sections.heading: Virtual Admittance and Reinforcement Learning: Synthesizing Feasible Whole-Body Compliance
sections.summary: Virtual torques derived from kinematic chain deflections drive a virtual admittance system, and whole-body IK synthesizes physically feasible tracking motions at scale. Using this data, teacher-student reinforcement learning trains a policy to drive whole-body joints in real time using only proprioceptive sensing.
sections.details:
The proposed LAC pipeline consists of three core components: problem formulation, compliant motion augmentation, and reinforcement learning.

■ III-A Problem Formulation
The robot receives base velocity commands $\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{cmd}}$, base height commands $h^{\mathrm{cmd}}$, and upper-body reference joint angles $\mathbf{q}^{\mathrm{ref}}$ (11 DoF). In addition, it takes a 5D stiffness command comprising a shared linear and angular stiffness pair for the left arm links $(K_{\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{rob}}, K_{\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{rob},\theta})$, a right arm pair $(K_{\mathrm{R}}^{\mathrm{rob}}, K_{\mathrm{R}}^{\mathrm{rob},\theta})$, and a torso (waist) linear stiffness $K_{\mathrm{T}}^{\mathrm{rob}}$. Because the torso has only one yaw axis, no angular stiffness is assigned to it. When subjected to unobserved external forces and couples, the robot compliantly yields according to these 5D stiffness commands while coordinating all 23 whole-body joints to maintain balance.

■ III-B Compliant Motion Augmentation
To generate training data, contact data from human-object interactions (OMOMO dataset) and human-human interactions (Inter-X dataset) are retargeted to the robot to extract contact frames. Trapezoidal force and couple profiles are then applied to these base poses.
- Ensuring physical consistency in rotation: This is the central design innovation. Instead of directly driving link rotations with external torques, forces are mapped through the Jacobian across the downstream joint chain from the contact point, yielding passive deflection angles $\Delta\mathbf{q}_u$ governed by the hardware joint PD stiffness $\Lambda_q$. The resulting link orientation deviation $\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_j$ in this deflected pose is converted into a virtual torque $\boldsymbol{\tau}_j^{\mathrm{vir}} = \kappa \Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_j$ that drives the admittance system. Consequently, when the commanded angular stiffness is $K_j^{\mathrm{rob},\theta} = \kappa$, the motion matches the passive arm deflection exactly; setting it lower yields a larger rotation, and setting it higher yields a smaller one, anchoring stiffness modulation to a grounded physical reference.
- Whole-body IK and feasibility checking: Target poses from the virtual second-order admittance model at each contact link are solved via whole-body differential IK using quadratic programming (QP). The solved motions are verified to confirm whether commanded stiffness is satisfied (force error $\le 5\text{ N}$, torque error $\le 1.5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$) and that no self-collisions occur. If constraints are violated, forces are gradually decayed and recomputed. Through this process, a high-quality dataset of roughly 1,050 hours (378,051 episodes) was generated.

■ III-C Reinforcement Learning on Augmented Data
Training employs a two-stage RMA-style teacher-student framework. In the first stage, PPO trains a privileged encoder receiving privileged information (external wrenches, true base velocities, tracking residuals, etc.) alongside an actor that takes short observation histories and latent representations. Concurrently, an estimator is trained via regression to predict this latent representation using only a 64-frame (1.28-second) history of proprioceptive measurements. In the second stage, the actor is frozen and deployed as a student policy using the estimator's output. Symmetry augmentation to prevent left-right bias and resampling to increase data for less-frequently contacted links (shoulders and elbows) are also incorporated.

sections.heading: Validation in Simulation and on Unitree G1: Continuous Stiffness Modulation and Whole-Body Coordination
sections.summary: In both simulation and real hardware, varying linear and angular stiffness produced designed, monotonic modulations in link displacements and rotation angles. LAC outperformed baselines by taking steps to avoid falling and offering a significantly wider range of stiffness tuning.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted in simulation (MuJoCo) and on the real 23-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid robot.

■ IV-A Efficacy of Linear and Angular Compliance
- Linear stiffness validation: When varying the left arm's linear stiffness from 10 N/m to 500 N/m under a 20 N peak force applied in anterior-posterior, lateral, and downward directions, displacement of the center of mass decreased monotonically as stiffness increased. Meanwhile, the link's orientation remained virtually unchanged, proving that linear and angular compliance operate independently.
- Angular stiffness validation: Arm angular stiffness was varied from 10 to 100 N·m/rad under applied couples (4 N·m) and pulling forces. Increasing stiffness from 10 to 100 caused the hand's orientation change under couples to decrease monotonically from 60 degrees to 17 degrees. Pulling tests with a force gauge on the real robot matched simulation orientation curves remarkably well, demonstrating sim-to-real transfer.

■ IV-B Baseline Comparisons
LAC was compared against SoftMimic, GentleHumanoid, and FALCON. When pulled forward-downward with up to 40 N from a quiet stance, SoftMimic and GentleHumanoid attempted to keep their lower bodies in place, causing their feet to lift and hop forward. FALCON, built for robust tracking, showed no compliance and slipped. In contrast, LAC extended its arms while autonomously stepping forward and lowering its center of mass to absorb the force, smoothly returning to its stance once the load was released.
In quantitative benchmarks (hand pull, elbow pull, torso push), only LAC maintained monotonic displacement reductions across all stiffness commands, achieving the widest modulation range (up to 49 cm on the compliant end and down to 8 cm on the stiff end).

■ IV-C Real-World Task Performance
On the real G1, coordinated whole-body responses were verified: the robot walked forward when its arm was pulled and bent its knees to lower its body when its torso was pushed. Under manual wrist twisting, the wrist rotated 84 degrees under low angular stiffness versus only 15 degrees under high angular stiffness. When a 4 kg object was placed on its forearm, low angular stiffness caused the arm to tilt and drop the object, whereas high angular stiffness kept the arm level for stable carrying. Furthermore, LAC handled practical loco-manipulation tasks via VR teleoperation, including carrying a yoga ball (soft setting to prevent crushing), carrying a heavy box, and pushing open a door (stiff settings to exert substantial forces).

sections.heading: Summary and Future Directions: Autonomous Adaptation and Other Platforms
sections.summary: Combining large-scale compliant motion augmentation with reinforcement learning, LAC establishes whole-body linear and angular compliance across a humanoid's upper body. Future directions include context-driven automatic stiffness adaptation, tactile sensor integration, and extensions to wheeled or quadrupedal platforms.
sections.details:
This work proposed and validated LAC, an integrated controller that achieves commanded whole-body linear and angular compliance on a humanoid robot by combining large-scale data augmentation with teacher-student reinforcement learning. Achieving compliant interactions through whole-body degrees of freedom alongside a broad modulation range marks a significant step forward.

The authors highlight three directions for future work:
- Autonomous stiffness adjustment: Currently, stiffness commands are manually specified by human operators; future iterations should enable the robot to determine appropriate stiffness dynamically based on visual perception and task context.
- Integration of tactile sensing: Incorporating tactile and contact sensors alongside current proprioceptive feedback (joint positions and velocities) to improve external wrench estimation accuracy.
- Application to other mobile manipulators: Because lower-body control is decoupled through base velocity and height interfaces, a similar methodology can be applied to quadrupeds with mounted arms or wheeled mobile manipulators.

takeaways: Anchoring angular compliance targets to the passive deflections of the downstream joint chain—rather than isolated links—enables physically consistent and proprioceptively observable motion synthesis.

Independently commanding linear and angular stiffness allows sophisticated physical interactions, such as yielding to wrist twisting while maintaining hand position or keeping arms horizontal while carrying objects.
When subjected to external wrenches, having the lower body autonomously step or adjust base height alongside upper-body joints prevents falls and naturally absorbs disturbances across the whole body.
limitations: The 5D stiffness parameters must currently be specified manually by a human operator, lacking autonomous adaptation to changing task contexts.

External wrench detection relies on estimating forces from proprioceptive histories (such as joint deflections), which limits sensitivity to small contact forces or distributed surface contacts (tactile integration remains future work).
The torso link possesses only a single yaw axis, so angular compliance is not designed for it, restricting its compliance strictly to translational directions.
